lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, well. Alexander. [pause] You're dead too, then. Like the rest of us.
lines.note: Flat delivery. The running gag opening — 'so you're dead too' — lands as a statement of fact, not a greeting.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: As you can see, Diogenes. Not so surprising, is it? I was human. Humans die.
lines.note: Slightly defensive. He's been rehearsing this reasonable tone.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So Ammon was lying, then. When he said you were his son. Turns out you were Philip's all along.
lines.note: Not a question. A bureaucratic observation.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Philip's. Obviously. If I were Ammon's son, I wouldn't be dead.
lines.note: The logic is airtight. He resents admitting it.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: There was also the story about your mother. That a serpent used to visit her — seen in her bed, if I recall — and that's how you were conceived, and Philip was deceived into thinking the child was his.
lines.note: Delivered as if reciting a mildly interesting historical footnote.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I heard all of that. Same as you did. But now I can see clearly enough — neither my mother nor the priests of Ammon were telling the truth.
lines.note: Weary. He's moved past indignation into something more like resignation.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, the lie wasn't entirely useless to you, Alexander. A lot of men grovelled because they thought you were a god. Practical, really.
lines.note: Genuine acknowledgement, but the compliment is entirely forensic.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell me — who did you leave that enormous empire to?
lines.note: Seamless pivot, no pause for sentiment.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I don't know, Diogenes. I didn't manage to give any instructions about it. Only this — as I was dying, I gave Perdiccas my ring. [pause] But why are you laughing?
lines.note: The irritation at the laughter is sincere.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Oh, I was just remembering how Greece behaved when you first took power — all that flattery, electing you their champion, their general against the barbarians. Some of them even added you to the twelve gods. Built you temples. Sacrificed to you as the son of a serpent. [chuckles] That's all.
lines.note: The list is delivered with the fond amusement of someone cataloguing minor absurdities.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But tell me — where did the Macedonians bury you?
lines.note: Again, no transition. He is genuinely curious in the way a man might ask about a wine region.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I'm still lying in Babylon. This is the thirtieth day. Ptolemy the bodyguard has promised that once he gets a moment's peace from the chaos on his hands, he'll take me to Egypt and bury me there — so I can become one of the Egyptian gods.
lines.note: He delivers this last part without apparent irony. He still thinks it might happen.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And you expect me not to laugh? Here you are in Hades, still making plans. Still hoping to become Anubis. Or perhaps Osiris. [pause] Listen — most divine one — let that go. Nobody who has crossed the lake and passed through the gate comes back up. Aeacus is not careless, and Cerberus is not the sort of dog you can charm.
lines.note: The mock-honorific 'most divine one' is the sharpest line in the exchange. Dry, not cruel.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: There is one thing I would genuinely like to know, though. How does it feel — when you think about everything you left behind up there? The bodyguards, the shield-bearers, the satraps. All that gold. Nations prostrating themselves before you. Babylon. Bactria. Those great war elephants. The honour, the fame — riding out in state with the white ribbon round your head and the purple cloak pinned at your shoulder. [pause] Does it hurt, when you think about it? [pause] Why are you crying, you fool? Didn't the great Aristotle teach you not to trust what Fortune hands you?
lines.note: The catalogue is deliberately gorgeous — let it land before the turn. The final question is not unkind. It is genuinely puzzled.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: The wise Aristotle. [pause] The most accomplished flatterer who ever lived, you mean. Leave Aristotle to me — I know exactly what he was. How much he extracted from me, what his letters were like, how he exploited my pride in my education — fawning, flattering, one moment praising my looks as though beauty were a component of virtue, the next pointing to my campaigns and my wealth. He thought wealth was a good too, conveniently enough — it saved him the embarrassment of taking money with nothing to show for it. A fraud, Diogenes. A clever craftsman of a fraud. [pause] The one thing I got from his wisdom was this: knowing how to grieve properly over losing what he taught me were the greatest goods in the world. The ones you just listed.
lines.note: This is Alexander's most articulate and most honest speech. The bitterness about Aristotle is genuine. The self-awareness in the final lines is also genuine — and makes it worse.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well — here's a remedy for your grief. Hellebore doesn't grow down here, but there is the water of Lethe. Go and drink it. Deep draughts. Then drink again. Drink as often as it takes — until you stop mourning the goods of Aristotle. [pause] Because I should mention: I can see Cleitus over there. And Callisthenes. And quite a few others. They're moving in your direction, and they look like they'd like a word — specifically to tear you apart for what you did to them. So I'd take that other path, if I were you. [pause] And drink deeply.
lines.note: Delivered with the helpful practicality of a man giving directions. The last two words are the punchline — same beat as the opening.
